extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; literary critics; general readers interested in poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Critical lecture guidance for evaluating and understanding the poetic qualities of Alexander Pope and John Dryden, and more broadly the distinction between 'poets of nature' and 'poets of art'. Emphasises criteria of imagination, style, versification, satire, and appropriateness to poetic class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate poets relative to their stylistic class (artificial vs natural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden and Pope are the great masters of the artificial style of poetry in our language ... those who stand at the head of that class, ought, perhaps, to rank higher than those who occupy an inferior place in a superior class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a poet, identify the style/class (e.g., artificial/fancy/wit vs natural/imaginative). Compare like with like: a leading practitioner within an inferior class can deserve high rank for producing excellence unique to that class. Consider originality and capacity to gratify a distinct faculty or class of readers as part of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and capacity to gratify different readers/faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the merit of a work not more by its inherent and absolute worth, than by its originality and capacity of gratifying a different faculty of the mind, or a different class of readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work's originality and the particular pleasure it gives (even to readers 'not of the highest class') count toward its merit; don't dismiss works that excel in novel ways because they aren't 'grand' in the same mode as other traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet of nature vs poet of art (definition and contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet of nature ... sympathises with whatever is beautiful, and grand, and impassioned in nature ... The poet of art represents things as they appear to the indifferent observer, stripped of prejudice and passion, or clothes the little with mock-dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to diagnose a poet's aims and strengths: 'poet of nature' = universal sympathy, imagination, and grandeur; 'poet of art' = refinement, observation, polish, and artificiality. Evaluate whether the poet achieves the aim appropriate to his type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative power of imagination (communion with nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of the imagination ... has its centre in the human soul, and makes the circuit of the universe... He sees things in their eternal beauty, for he sees them as they are; he feels them in their universal interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer poets whose imagination is 'representative'—able to evoke universal feelings and images that endure. Assess whether the poet's vision is expansive and sympathetic beyond personal idiosyncrasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of sympathy and universality vs personality/narrow circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope had an exact knowledge of all that he himself loved or hated, wished or wanted... He was the poet of personality and of polished life. That which was nearest to him, was the greatest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether a poet's material and feeling reach universal human concerns or remain stuck in personal, fashionable, or local flavours. Narrow, highly personal focus can be a strength in artifice but a limitation relative to universal poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness vs affectation in depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: He saw nature only dressed by art; he judged of beauty by fashion; he sought for truth in the opinions of the world... He preferred the artificial to the natural in external objects, because he had a stronger fellow-feeling with the self-love of the maker or proprietor of a gewgaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether depictions feel genuinely natural or are noticeably dressed up by fashion/affectation. Excessive artifice (making trivial things appear heroic) is defensible within mock-heroic genres but is an affectation if mistaken for real grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and restraint of passion/pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: The pathos is of that mild contemplative kind ... There is none of the fierceness of intemperate passion, none of the agony of mind and turbulence of action ... This would have destroyed the beauty of the whole picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether pathos and passion are appropriate in intensity to subject and style. Restraint can preserve beauty; ungoverned passion may produce 'fierceness' that clashes with poetic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of irony and gravity in satire/mock-heroic
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance between the concealed irony and the assumed gravity, is as nicely trimmed as the balance of power in Europe... It is the perfection of the mock-heroic!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For mock-heroic and satirical works, judge the precision of the balance between ironic tone and elevated diction. Effective mock-heroic makes the little great and the great little without confusing register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and felicity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The conciseness and felicity of the expression are equally remarkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value economy of phrase and felicitous turns of expression; concise, well-chosen language is a key mark of excellence (exemplified in Pope's works like Rape of the Lock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical rules vs living genius (dangers of school-bound criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical rules laid down are too much those of a school, and of a confined one... There is a cant in the present day about genius, as every thing in poetry: there was a cant in the time of Pope about sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware treating poetic rules as absolute; school-bound critical maxims can obscure living originality. Evaluate whether 'rules' aid or constrain the poem's vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification: smoothness, harmony, and technical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: The praise of his versification must be confined to its uniform smoothness and harmony... his rhymes are constantly defective, being rhymes to the eye instead of the ear; ... he continually changes the tenses in the same sentence for the purposes of the rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess versification for sonic integrity (rhymes that work to the ear), consistency of tense and syntax, and overall smooth harmonious flow. Penalise technical lapses such as visually perfect but aurally false rhymes or awkward tense shifts made to force a rhyme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammatical construction and legitimacy of ellipsis
rubrics_metrics.description: His grammatical construction is often lame and imperfect. In the Abelard and Eloise, he says-- 'There died the best of passions, Love and Fame.' This is not a legitimate ellipsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate grammatical correctness and whether ellipses or constructions are legitimate. Faulty grammar or forced omissions that confuse sense are defects even in otherwise elegant verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical portraiture: realism vs artful caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden seems to grapple with his antagonists, and to describe real persons; Pope seems to refine upon them in his own mind, and to make them out just what he pleases, till they are not real characters, but the mere driveling effusions of his spleen and malice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge satirical portraits by whether they engage with real character and fresh strokes (Dryden-style) or degenerate into imagined caricature and repetitive spleen (a charge made against Pope). Realistic, discriminating portraiture is stronger satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and sonority in versification
rubrics_metrics.description: It also contains the finest examples of varied and sounding versification... He has left the best character of Shakspeare that has ever been written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value variety and sonorous movement in lines; versification that varies rhythm and sound has power and musicality, especially in odes and epic/lyrical passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyrical poetry depends on selection and suitability to music/recital
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyrical poetry, of all others, bears the nearest resemblance to painting: it deals in hieroglyphics and passing figures, which depend for effect, not on the working out, but on the selection. It is equally fit to be said or sung; it is not equally good to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate lyrical pieces for the aptness of their images (selection over elaboration) and for whether they succeed in performance (recitation or song) as well as on the page. Look for loftiness and truth of character beyond mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of ornament and refined detail
rubrics_metrics.description: No pains are spared, no profusion of ornament, no splendour of poetic diction, to set off the meanest things... The most glittering appearance is given to every thing, to paste, pomatum, billet-doux, and patches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether ornamentation and refined detail suit the poem's aim: lavish polish can be brilliantly apt (as in mock-heroic) but, if misapplied, becomes mere affectation. Judge balance and economy in ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of feeling and rhetorical eloquence in epistolary/lyric pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: The epistle of Eloise to Abelard ... It is fine as a poem: it is finer as a piece of high-wrought eloquence. The tears shed are drops gushing from the heart: the words are burning sighs breathed from the soul of love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For poetic letters/eloquent personae, value authentic, heartfelt feeling conveyed with rhetorical power. Emotional truth and eloquence can elevate verse even when derived from prior sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity and taste in translation/adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: His alterations from Chaucer and Boccaccio shew a greater knowledge of the taste of his readers and power of pleasing them, than acquaintance with the genius of his authors. He ekes out the lameness of the verse in the former, and breaks the force of the passion in both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate translations/adaptations for faithfulness to the original's force and feeling. Changes that suit contemporary taste are legitimate, but avoid alterations that blunt the original passion or essential genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power and vehemence of invective in satire ('magnanimity of abuse')
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a magnanimity of abuse in some of these epithets, a fearless choice of topics of invective, which may be considered as the heroical in satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether satirical invective is courageous, discriminating, and energetically applied; bold, well-aimed abuse can be a strength when used with purpose and discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual judgement of poetic decline and shifts in mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry had, at the period of which we are speaking, in general declined, by successive gradations, from the poetry of imagination ... to the poetry of fancy ... and again from the poetry of fancy to that of wit ... It degenerated into the poetry of mere common places ... transformed ... into the poetry of paradox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place poets and works in historical context: assess whether a poet exemplifies a transitional mode, decline, or revival. Historical changes in taste affect style and must be accounted for in evaluation rather than attributing all defects to individual failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters and prose as indicators of moral character and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope's letters and prose writings neither take away from, nor add to his poetical reputation... They, however, give a very favourable idea of his moral character in all respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prose and correspondence to inform judgments about a poet's character and rhetorical skill, but treat them as supplementary to poetic achievement rather than determinative.
